msItem.incipit: Peace to thy soul whilst we here moan

abstract.p: The poem mourns the death of Dr Johnson, an “honest” and “learned” physician; contrasting his virtue with the ignorance and hypocrisy of others who continue to practise. While the speaker praises the deceased for his integrity, he criticizes surviving doctors as unlearned, self-serving, and morally corrupt, failing to uphold the standards of their profession. The poem presents his death as an unjust reversal, in which the worthy are taken while the unworthy remain, and concludes with the broader reflection that experience shows the best die first while the worst continue to live.

lg.l: Peace to thy soule, Whylst Wee heere mone
With a just teare that Johnson’s gone;
How many yet survives scarse Knowes
Weether Gallen writt in verse or prose?
And yett these men still live; and can
Maintaine theire Footcloths, and their man;
They Physicke bodies but in vaine
They live to lust, and sinne to gaine:
They looke like saintes, and yett are looth
A Fortune that it should bee said
That these men live now Johnson’s deade!
But Practise doth this lesson give
The Best first dy, the Worst still live.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Thomas Johnson (c.1578–1621) was a physician based in Oxford. The son of a Bedfordshire gentleman, he matriculated at St Alban Hall in 1594 aged sixteen, proceeding BA from Oriel College in 1596 and MA in 1601 (incorporated at Cambridge in 1604). He supplicated for a licence to practise medicine on 13 June 1608 and was awarded the degrees of Bachelor and Doctor of Medicine on 26 June 1609. He resided in the parish of St Mary Magdalen and was buried at St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, on 16 November 1621(Oxfordshire Medics)
